Tne majority of piezometers installed in tne Po Shan area have only
been monitored since June 1983, amd they were read only manually
throughout the 1983 wet season. It appears from these readings, and those
fron a few piezometers installed during earlier studies, that storm
responses are not as important as seasonal piezometric rises. Following a
wet start to the year, the piezometric contours were high (Figures 17 and
18), and it is thought unlikely that water levels would rise beyond these
by more than 1 m seasonally and 1.5 m due to stonns of a 1 in 10 year
return period.

4.1.2 Flow in the Main Water Table

Fron the measured piezometric levels within the main water table and
the contoured pedrock profile, an analysis of flow direction and rate was
carried out using tne mean value of pemneability derived fran the pumping
test. This was done by dividing tne area into a series of square blocks
on a 15 m grid spacing. The flow tnrough the sides of each plock was
estimated using Darcy's law, corrections peing made for slope geometry.
These values were used to determine an average flow rate and direction
througn each olock. A computer programne was written to carry out these
calculations.

The accuracy of tne flow estimates are thought to ce low because of
variations in permeanility of the ground and flow tnrough pedrock. It was
not possible to take these factors into account in the analysis. ‘Tne
results are presented in Figure 21. Tnis bears a close resemplance in
fomn to Figure 20, whicn shows the wetted thickness apove pedrock. Of
particular significance is the variation of flow downslope petween flow
lines. It appears. that flow through bedrock may account for this
variation, which is particularly noticeable around boreholes PD20 and PD26
where tne wetted thickness has been shown to decrease. However, the
concept of flow through bedrock at this location is in conflict with the
results fron tne pumping test, wnich indicate tnat the area in question
behaves as an imperfect barrier. Some of this flow deficit in the area of
PD20 and PD26 may be accounted for py flow into the perched water table
which exists in this area. The major part, however, almost certainly
results from variations in the ground permeability.

4.1.3 Perched Water Tables

The two areas indicated in Figure 18 had consistent percned water
taples throughout tne wet season. These areas are in the vicinity of
boreholes PD33 and ML? on tne west side and poreholes PD14, P15, PD20 and
ML6 on the eastern side. Perching apparently occurred at the base of the
colluvium. In the case of the eastern side perched water table, it would
sean tnat, wnen the main water taole is nigh, the phreatic surface rises
above the colluvium pase, leading to a split in groundwater flow vetween
tne main and perched water tables. This additional flow in the perched
water taple nelps, in part, to account for the deficit in the amount of
water flowing in tne main aquifer in this region, as shown in Figure 21.
